summary: Round 7 delta is comment deletions plus two assertions becoming absolute; no production byte changed. All four things I was asked to verify hold, measured rather than accepted. (1) 17 is CORRECT and STABLE: full suite green at 786 tests, and the two bounded suites re-run three times with --rerun-tasks stay green. (2) The named mutant `epoch != ownEpoch && crossFromCheckpoint(hops, epoch, upTo)` fails exactly six tests in my own tree, and the two newly-absolute assertions are two of them (expected 17L but was 16L) -- so the change kills a mutant the previous relative form admitted. Making them absolute also pins the CONSTANT part of the budget, not only its slope, which is more than the mutant named and is the right direction. (3) Nothing load-bearing was lost by the deletions: the `26L` note still carries its reason (the off-by-one measured at 27 under `<= 30`), and the correctness suite's new javadoc is hedged ("Some tests here also count requests") so it cannot be falsified by moving an assertion -- the right form. (4) Nothing broke. Three MINORS, all documentation, none blocking. Two are surviving instances of the very sentence form the delta exists to remove, at sites the author asked me to check: ADR-0035 and the backlog row. The third is a navigational pointer that was deleted alongside the stale clause it shared a sentence with. Also noted, not filed: the two new assertions `assertThat(oneTerm.total()).isEqualTo(17L)` and `assertThat(shortChain.total()).isEqualTo(17L)` carry no `.as()` label, unlike every other cost assertion in these two suites -- under the mutant they were the only two of the six failures whose message was a bare number.

findings.blocks_rationale: Documentation only. No production code, no test assertion and no cost budget is affected, and review.md `minors-land` says a minor on a pass is recorded and lands. Recording it rather than fixing it is also what `minors-land` prescribes, since the fix would be fresh prose that becomes round 8's surface.
findings.title: A cross-file inventory of another suite's assertions SURVIVES in ADR-0035, and this delta made it staler
findings.detail: The ADR says: 'What actually fails is `aCheckpointSittingEXACTLYOnTheBarrierIsUsed`, whose exact count goes 18 to 17, and the failover totals.' That is exactly the sentence form this round deleted from the two suites -- an inventory of which assertions in other files fail under a variant. I applied that variant (`epoch != ownEpoch && crossFromCheckpoint(hops, epoch, upTo)`) in my own tree and ran `:sequencer:test`: SIX tests fail, not two. LocalSequencerBoundedRecoveryTest.takeoverCostIsCONSTANTInTheNumberOfPriorTerms (17->16), .takeoverCostIsCONSTANTInTheLengthOfTheAncestorsChain (17->16), .aPredecessorTOOSHORTToCheckpointStillStopsAtItsAncestorsCheckpoint (26->25), BoundedRecoveryCorrectnessTest.aCheckpointSittingEXACTLYOnTheBarrierIsUsed (18->17), .aRunOfBURNEDEpochsStillStopsAtTheCheckpointBehindThem, and LocalSequencerFailoverTest.aTakeoverReadsEveryEntryOfEveryANCESTORAndTHATISAREGRESSION. Two of those six were made to fail BY THIS DELTA. The sentence was already incomplete when written (it omits aRunOfBURNEDEpochs and aPredecessorTOOSHORT, both already absolute at the previous hash), which is the predicted decay rather than an accident.
findings.suggested: If touched at all, replace the enumeration with the property -- the own-epoch probe is pinned by exact request counts on the bounded path -- rather than restating the list, since restating produces a fresh sentence with the same decay property.
findings.failure_scenario: A later session wants the stat back -- ADR-0035's own Decision section prices the own-epoch probe at one stat per takeover and its Alternatives section is where that trade is argued. It reads 'What actually fails is aCheckpointSittingEXACTLYOnTheBarrierIsUsed ... and the failover totals', applies the variant to see how narrow the objection really is, and gets a failure set that does not match the ADR. It then has to decide whether the ADR's measurement was ever made -- which is the same 'stale numbers under the word MEASURED' failure this ADR's own warning banner records for its before-column, reappearing one section lower. The direction is safe (more tests protect the probe than the ADR claims, so nobody is misled into deleting it), which is why this is minor and not major.

findings.blocks_rationale: Documentation only, inside a chronological row whose later bullets explicitly supersede it, and the row is archived rather than loaded by every session (check-session-load.sh passed on an open-rows-only backlog). review.md `minors-land`.
findings.title: The M4.9 row still asserts the inventory its own later bullets falsify
findings.detail: The staged row contains, in present tense: 'AND THE ONLY ABSOLUTE COST ASSERTION ON THE BOUNDED PATH IS NEW: every other one compares two measurements, which a recovery issuing six redundant requests satisfies.' Two bullets later the same row says 'EVERY COST ASSERTION ON THE BOUNDED PATH IS NOW EXACT' and, in the bullet this delta added, 'AND THE LAST TWO RELATIVE ASSERTIONS ARE ABSOLUTE'. The row also still carries 'killed only by exact counts in the sibling file' as a live clause while a later bullet quotes that same clause as one of the six specimens of the defect being removed. So the row states, as fact, two sentences it later names as the shape it deleted.
findings.suggested: Nothing, unless the row is edited for another reason. If it is, the earlier clause is the one to edit -- patching the later one is what produced the previous six instances.
findings.failure_scenario: A session picks up follow-up work on the bounded-recovery suites, reads the M4.9 row from backlog-done.md to reconstruct what was decided, and stops at the first cost bullet. It concludes the bounded path is mostly pinned by relative comparisons and either (a) writes a new relative assertion believing that is the house style here, or (b) reports the suite as weaker than it is. Both are cheap to recover from because the contradicting bullet is in the same row, which is why this is minor.

findings.blocks_rationale: Navigational documentation. No assertion, no budget and no production behaviour depends on it, and the link still exists in the other direction (LocalSequencerFailoverTest and CheckpointCursor both name the cost suite). review.md `minors-land`.
findings.title: The deletion took the split pair's only forward pointer with it
findings.detail: The deleted sentence was two claims welded together: a NAME ('{@code LocalSequencerBoundedRecoveryTest} asserts request counts') and an inventory ('and every assertion here asserts offsets'). Only the second had the decay property. Both went. The javadoc now opens 'THE COST SUITE IS SATISFIED BY A RECOVERY THAT READS NOTHING AND IS WRONG, which is why this half exists' with no statement anywhere in the file of which file the cost suite is -- I grepped: BoundedRecoveryCorrectnessTest.java contains no reference to LocalSequencerBoundedRecoveryTest. The names do not parallel either (LocalSequencerBoundedRecoveryTest / BoundedRecoveryCorrectnessTest), so it is not guessable. The M4.9 row records this pair as a deliberate 500-line-gate split into COST and CORRECTNESS around a shared fixture; that seam is now documented from one side only.
findings.suggested: If restored, restore only the name and not the inventory -- '{@code LocalSequencerBoundedRecoveryTest} is the cost half' cannot be falsified by moving an assertion, which is the property the delta is selecting for.
findings.failure_scenario: A maintainer adding a bounded-recovery test opens BoundedRecoveryCorrectnessTest, reads that 'THE COST SUITE' is what this half exists to backstop, cannot find which file that is, and adds a request-count assertion here -- or, worse, concludes the cost half does not exist and writes a duplicate of it. The shared BoundedRecoveryFixture makes that easy to do and hard to notice.

cost_lens: No production code in this delta, so no request can have been added. The delta moves the bounded-path cost pins from relative to absolute, which strengthens the request-rate gate rather than weakening it: a relative pair is satisfied by any constant overhead, an absolute total is not. Measured: 17 total requests at 1 prior term and at 16, and at 12 entries and at 60 -- flat in terms and in entries, which is the non-negotiable-6 shape. Nothing here scales with records, shards, partitions or indices.
